title: We're doctors who may be posted anywhere. Should we buy a home in JB?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #196 | GET A HOME ONLY WHEN YOU NEED IT
excerpt: Two government doctors in JB with a baby on the way weigh a condo near the hospital against a strata landed home further out. Sean says rent close to work and buy a home only when you need it.

qa.asker: W, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: W, 35, and his wife, 33, are newly qualified medical specialists in government service in JB, on call at night and expecting a baby. They will stay in JB for at least two years, after which he may be posted elsewhere for three to four years of training, followed by a seven-year bond before private practice. They are weighing a condo 15 minutes from work against a RM700,000 to RM800,000 strata landed home in Mount Austin, 30 to 40 minutes away, while JB condo prices keep falling.
qa.question: Should they buy a condo near the hospital now and upgrade to landed later, or buy the landed home?
qa.quote: I should get that particular home just in time when I need it.
qa.answer: Prioritise flexibility. Rent an apartment close to the hospital, which is cheap while JB condo prices are low, and don't tie themselves to a home they may have to leave. If they want property, buy it purely as an investment that generates cash flow, and buy the family home in their early 40s once their careers settle and their child needs space.

reasons.title: Postings make ownership a burden
reasons.body: If they are sent to another state soon after buying, they end up renting the house out, maintaining it from afar and topping up the instalment. A rented flat near work lets them get home quickly between calls.

reasons.title: Babies need convenience, not a big house
reasons.body: A single-level apartment makes it easier to feed, clean and work while the baby sleeps, and pools and playgrounds downstairs are what young children enjoy. Space and privacy matter later, around ages 10 to 12.

reasons.title: JB high-rise and landed behave differently
reasons.body: Condos were built largely for Singapore investors and have fallen in value, partly through oversupply, while landed homes stay expensive because many Malaysians working in Singapore buy them for their families.

reasons.title: A home bought early rarely makes money
reasons.body: Interest and instalments over 15 years account for much of a house's rise in value. A rental property that tenants pay for builds equity even without capital gains, and can be sold later to fund the family home.

actions: Rent an apartment within a short drive of the hospital.
If they invest, judge each JB project only on whether its rent covers the instalment.
Add a second rental property after two or three years if the first works.
Buy the long-term family home once private practice and their child's needs are clear.
As government employees, look into the LPPSA housing loan.
qa.caveat: If having their own home now is a real need for the family rather than fear of missing out, buying is a legitimate choice. Sean also notes property may not suit them at all, and stocks, bonds or ETFs could be more flexible.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #196. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in January 2023. Sean says he is a VIP member of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase company linked in the video description.
